sections.title: Positioning
sections.summary: Stripe presents itself as programmable financial infrastructure for businesses of any size, not as a store builder. The same frame runs from the homepage through the startup, enterprise and platform pages.
keyPoints: Homepage promise: accept payments, handle business banking and build custom revenue models, 'from your first transaction to your billionth'.
Each audience gets its own page: startups (a program with credits and perks), enterprises (named customers and volume figures) and platforms (Connect).
Nothing in the surveyed navigation speaks to a small store owner directly.

sections.title: Products and offerings
sections.summary: A 53-product catalogue in eight areas: payments, risk, revenue, data, money management, embedded finance, stablecoins and crypto, and the platform itself. A recommender helps visitors who don't know where to start.
keyPoints: Many product names are insider terms (Authorization Boost, Data Pipeline), so the index leans on filters by use case and product area.

rows: Online, in-person and agent-led payments, with a prebuilt, customizable checkout
Merchant of record: takes on tax, fraud and disputes
In-person payments with precertified card readers
Payments for platforms and marketplaces; Shopify and DoorDash are named users
Loans and merchant cash advances, repaid as a share of daily sales

gaps: Tax, Treasury, Issuing and the crypto products were in the navigation but not opened.

sections.title: Pricing
sections.summary: Pay as you go with published per-transaction rates and no plan fee, plus a custom lane for large volume or unusual business models. Add-ons carry their own monthly or per-event fees.
keyPoints: Stripe states there are no setup, monthly or hidden fees on standard pricing.
Custom pricing (interchange-plus, volume, multi-product and country-specific rates) goes through sales.

rows: 30% of the disputed amount, only when you win

gaps: Billing, Tax, Radar and Connect prices were not on the pricing page text.
No all-in cost estimate; the visitor adds fees across products.

sections.title: Merchandising
sections.summary: Stripe merchandises its own offer as two lanes: a standard rate shown first as the default, and a custom lane through sales. For merchants it supplies pricing and checkout models rather than catalogue tools.
keyPoints: The pricing page puts the white Standard card beside a dark Custom card with four levers, so self-serve reads as the default and sales as the exception.
Standard-rate customers get several features at no extra charge.
The product index offers filters and a 'Get a recommendation' helper for visitors who don't know what to pick.
Merchant tools shown: no-code payment links, a customizable checkout, and Billing's usage-based and subscription pricing models.
Not shown: catalogue, collections, product search or recommendation tooling. Stripe sells the payment layer, not a storefront.

sections.title: Technical platform
sections.summary: The strongest part of the site: a public REST API reference with sandboxes, dated and named releases, SDKs, a CLI, an app and extension model, and AI-agent tooling, all readable logged out.
keyPoints: REST API with JSON and standard HTTP verbs; sandboxes let developers test without touching live data.
Official client libraries in seven languages: Ruby, Python, PHP, Java, Node.js, Go and .NET.
Public changelog with dated, named API versions; the latest listed is 2026-11-18, named Endive.
Developer tools listed include the CLI, Workbench, Terraform and a Visual Studio Code extension.
Extension model: Stripe apps, extensions and custom objects. AI tooling: Model Context Protocol and agent skills.
Stated limit: the API does not support bulk updates, so one object per request.
gaps: Rate limits, webhook reliability and SLAs were not read.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: Large, confident type on a single typeface, a purple accent and gradient ribbons as the signature graphic. The marketing site is tightly built; the pricing page and docs drift from it in small ways.
keyPoints: One typeface (sohne-var) and one primary button give each page a single focus.
Two purples are in use: #533afd on the home page and #635bff on the pricing page.
Button corners are 4px on the home page and 16.5px on pricing; the API reference sets text in the system font.
On the home page a gradient ribbon runs through the headline, crossing words such as 'your revenue' and 'banking'.
The pricing page is long, 23,309px tall, with the Standard and Custom cards as its focal point.
For merchants, Checkout is described as customizable; no theme or brand-kit tooling was surveyed.
gaps: Dark mode and motion were not assessed.

sections.title: Company presentation
sections.summary: A mission-led story about economic growth, with proof from named customer outcomes and very large aggregate numbers. The volume figures are worded differently from page to page.
keyPoints: Mission: build programmable financial infrastructure to make it easier and cheaper for any business to start and scale.
Scale claims: more than 5 million businesses, around 1.8% of global GDP, and $1.9 trillion in volume on the Enterprise page.
The Customers page says Stripe processes 'hundreds of billions of dollars each year'; the About page says 'trillions'.
Customer proof leads with outcomes: a $70M revenue increase at Postmates, a 10% acceptance uplift at Twilio, and Intercom going live on usage-based billing in 3 months.
gaps: No leadership or investor information in the surveyed pages.

jtbd_fit.evidence: Home names the jobs (accept payments, business banking, custom revenue models); Startups, Enterprise and Platforms pages each name a segment job.

capability_visible.evidence: Public API reference, changelog and product index with in-page UI demos are all readable logged out. The account dashboard sits behind signup.

pricing_transparency.evidence: Standard card, in-person, dispute, hardware and Managed Payments rates are published. Billing, Tax and IC+ rates are not on the captured text.

product_breadth.evidence: 53 products grouped into eight areas, with a recommender for the lost visitor. Many product names are jargon (Authorization Boost, Data Pipeline).

platform_depth.evidence: REST reference, seven SDK languages, sandboxes, named versions, CLI, apps and extensions, MCP and agent skills are all public.

time_to_value.evidence: Capture stops at the account form; first-payment time was not observed.

friction.evidence: One click from home to the form. Form asks email, full name, password and country, with Google as an alternative.

trust.evidence: Named customers (Twilio, Atlassian, Intercom, Shopify, DoorDash) with specific outcomes. Uptime claim is unsourced.

mobile.evidence: Phone captures exist for home and pricing but were not assessed.

states.evidence: No error or empty states reached.

value_prop_clarity.evidence: Clear to developers and finance leads. 'Financial infrastructure' does not tell a first-time store owner what to do.

proof_quality.evidence: Case stats are named and specific, but the headline GDP ticker has no source and payment-method counts differ by page (100+, 125+, 75+).

persuasion_integrity.evidence: No countdowns or scarcity. A promo rate is labelled with an end date.

cta_logic.evidence: 'Get started' is primary with 'Sign up with Google' and 'Contact sales' ranked below it; pricing page repeats the pattern per tier.

company_narrative.evidence: Same infrastructure story from home to About to Enterprise. Volume is stated as 'trillions' on About but 'hundreds of billions' on Customers.

offer_packaging.evidence: Standard and custom lanes are clear and each product fee is listed separately. 53 products and per-product fee tables make total cost hard to add up.

offer_architecture.evidence: Self-serve default rate, add-ons, a startup program and a volume lane through sales form a deliberate ladder. There is no entry trial because there is no plan fee.

merchant_merch_tools.evidence: No-code payment links, Checkout and Billing's pricing models are shown. Catalogue, search and recommendation tools are not part of the offer.

visual_craft.evidence: Strong hierarchy: one typeface, large headline, one primary button. The ribbon crossing the headline costs some legibility.

system_coherence.evidence: Two purples (#533afd and #635bff), button corners of 4px on home and 16.5px on pricing, and system-font docs show small drifts between pages.

merchant_design_control.evidence: Checkout is described as customizable and Elements is a listed product; no theme or brand-kit tooling was surveyed.

read.summary: A developer-grade platform with unusually open docs and a published rate card, sold to a broad audience with one infrastructure story. It under-serves the small merchant who lands on the homepage.
pros: Pricing is public and specific, down to dispute and hardware fees.
The API reference, changelog and tooling are readable without an account.
Named customers carry specific outcome numbers.
Signup is one click and one short form from home.
cons: A 53-product catalogue with insider names is hard to navigate for a newcomer.
The homepage GDP ticker and the payment-method counts (100+, 125+, 75+) are not reconciled or sourced.
No all-in cost view; the visitor adds fees across add-ons.
Nothing in the nav speaks to a small store owner.
read.howItSells: Sells credibility and scale: infrastructure language, a very large numbers frame, and named enterprise logos. Then widens by segment (startups, enterprise, platforms) with a program or sales contact for each.
copy: Publish the rate card including the awkward fees.
Keep the API reference and changelog public.
Pair every primary CTA with a sales route for large buyers.
avoid: A live stat with no source.
Different headline counts for the same capability on different pages.
unknowns: What happens after account creation and how long to a first payment.
Billing, Tax, Radar and Connect prices.
Whether the 53-product index helps or overwhelms a real first-time visitor.

hypothesis.statement: A small-merchant path from the homepage (a 'Take your first payment today' card leading to Payment Links) will raise signup completion among non-developer visitors.
hypothesis.metric: Signup-start to account-created rate for non-developer traffic
hypothesis.guardrail: Developer-segment signup rate and sales-contact volume
hypothesis.decisionRule: Ship to the segment if completion rises by a pre-agreed margin over two weeks and the developer rate holds.

merchandising.summary: A clean two-lane offer with the standard rate as the default and sales as the exception. The weakness is the number of separate fee tables, not the packaging of any one product.
pros: The standard rate is the first thing on the pricing page, and the custom lane is clearly separate.
The product index lets a lost visitor filter or ask for a recommendation.
Add-ons are described as included with the standard rate.
cons: Fees are spread across products with no all-in estimate.
53 products are listed with insider names.
No catalogue or storefront merchandising tools are presented.

design.summary: Confident and consistent on the home page, looser on the pricing page and docs. The ribbon is the one decision that hurts: it sits behind the headline it should be supporting.
pros: A single typeface and a single primary button give each page one focus.
The Standard and Custom cards contrast on purpose.
Merchants get real design control over checkout.
cons: The gradient ribbon crosses the home headline.
Two purple accents and two button shapes between home and pricing.
Docs switch to the system font.

claims.text: Businesses see 2x growth in payment volume on average.
No setup fees, monthly fees, or hidden fees.
More than 5 million businesses build on Stripe
Intercom takes only 3 months to implement usage-based billing with Stripe.
Pay one flat fee that never changes. There are no compounding interest charges, or late fees.
hundreds of billions of dollars each year

signupPath: 'Get started' opens dashboard.stripe.com/register, a real account form: email, full name, password and country, with a 'Create account' button and a Google sign-up option, shown over a demo dashboard. It took one click from the homepage. Nothing was entered, so what happens after account creation was not seen.
